passages.t: ‘The apple of Your eye’, and ‘when I awake’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A prayer of David” (verse 1). The man asks God to hear his case: “Hear, O LORD, my righteous plea; listen to my cry” (verse 1). He wants the verdict to come from God himself: “May my vindication come from Your presence; may Your eyes see what is right” (verse 2).

He says God has searched him already. “You have tried my heart; You have visited me in the night. You have tested me and found no evil” (verse 3).

Enemies surround him. They are “like a lion greedy for prey, like a young lion lurking in ambush” (verse 12). So he asks for shelter: “Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings” (verse 8). Then for action: “Arise, O LORD, confront them!” (verse 13).

The last verse looks past the enemies altogether. They are “men of the world whose portion is in this life” (verse 14). “As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is a lament from someone falsely accused. A ‘righteous plea’ is a court word: a just case. In Israel, cases were heard by the elders at the town gate. This man takes his case past the gate, to God.

The two pictures of verse 8 come from the Song of Moses. There God guarded Israel “as the apple of His eye” and, like an eagle, “spread His wings to catch them” (Deuteronomy 32:10-11). ‘The apple of the eye’ is the pupil, which in Hebrew is ‘the little man of the eye’: the tiny figure of yourself you see in someone else's eye. It is the part of the body everyone protects without thinking. The man asks to be that close to God, and that guarded.
passages.later:
The shelter of God's wings returns in Ruth, where Boaz blesses Ruth as one who came to the God of Israel “under whose wings you have taken refuge” (Ruth 2:12). Jesus used the picture of himself, grieving over Jerusalem: “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matthew 23:37).

The hope of verse 15, to see God's face on waking, grows clearer in the New Testament: “we will see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2).
passages.hard: ‘You have tested me and found no evil’ (verse 3) can sound proud. It is a claim to be innocent of the charge against him, not a claim never to have sinned. The book page explains this in the part ‘When a psalmist says he is innocent’.
passages.asks:
When you are falsely accused, the psalm teaches you to take the case to God rather than to fight it out in anger. That is hard, and it is freeing.

It also asks what your ‘portion’ is. The enemies' portion is ‘in this life’. The psalmist's is God's face. Pray verse 8 for yourself, or for a child, using the words of a parent who guards what they love most.
